source.title: GMoE: Global Mixture of Experts with Logit Propagation

record.file_problem: none; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The matched-parameter comparison reports held-out perplexity for different MoE architectures, bearing on whether architecture differences change performance at a fixed parameter count. It does not fit or test the stated scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The paper mentions scaling laws as background and says future work should examine whether GMoE aligns with scaling-law trends. It does not test parameter-, token-, or compute-scaling laws, extrapolation, compute-optimal allocation, or loss-to-downstream predictability. Table 8 is included because it compares held-out perplexity at a matched parameter count. Other performance tables compare models or methods for GMoE’s parameter-efficiency and benchmark claims, rather than testing the remaining claim versions.
record.test_reason: This is a method paper proposing GMoE. It cites Kaplan and Hoffmann only as background and leaves alignment with scaling-law trends to future work. Table 8 compares the authors' own architecture with downscaled baselines at matched total parameters. That is a method-versus-baseline comparison, not a test of V4. V4 concerns depth, width and shape at fixed non-embedding parameters within a wide range. Here the arms differ in routing design, MoE layer frequency and activated parameters: GMoE has 181M activated parameters, while the baselines, with FFN inner size cut to 731, have far fewer. No scaling fits, extrapolation, allocation or loss-to-downstream analysis is reported.
record.authors_conclusion: Essentially correct. The authors conclude that GMoE, using Global Experts shared across layers plus logit-propagating routing, reaches competitive perplexity and benchmark accuracy with substantially fewer parameters. They also say it mitigates path collapse. They leave it to future work to check that the gains persist at larger scale and fit scaling-law trends.
record.recipe_differences: The paper compares MoE architectures using matched-parameter perplexity; it does not use the original scaling-law fitting or compute-optimal allocation procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: The matched-parameter comparison is limited to the Base model and the four reported evaluation corpora.

fits_no_version.finding: At 204M total parameters (Base, 50B tokens), MoE routing designs differ in held-out perplexity: average 33.32 for GMoE versus 34.43–36.65 for the baselines. GMoE also has more activated parameters than the downscaled baselines.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For MoE models matched on total parameters, routing and expert-sharing design changes held-out loss by several percent.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Proceedings of the 64th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics, 2026)
record.problems: The paper does not fit scaling curves or measure compute-optimal allocations. The matched-parameter architecture comparison covers one model scale, reports no uncertainty estimates, and does not vary depth or width across a wide range.
record.rows_left_out: No other claim-relevant rows identified. The remaining tables report GMoE architecture, benchmark, ablation, routing, memory, or utilization results without testing the other claim versions.

untested.parts: No power-law fit of loss against parameters, tokens or compute. Only three dense/MoE sizes are trained, all at a fixed 50B tokens.
No variation of depth, width or shape at fixed non-embedding parameter count.
No other modality or training regime.
No relation of downstream accuracy to scale or loss is fitted. Tables 1–2 only list values for three sizes.
No comparison of exponents or fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V4 'challenges' label is removed. The comparison is a method paper's matched-parameter benchmark against its own baselines, confounded by activated parameters (compute) and MoE layer placement. It is not a shape sweep at fixed N. Table 1 shows perplexity falling from Small to Base to Large for every architecture, but with three points at fixed tokens and no fit, it is not a test of V1.

versions.untested_parts: Power-law relationships between held-out loss and parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether fits from small runs predict substantially larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its trend with compute.
The comparison covers Base-scale MoE architectures at a matched parameter count, not a wide range of depth, width, or other architecture settings.
Other modalities and training regimes, including repeated data, fine-tuning, and transfer.
No tested relationship between pretraining loss and downstream performance, or predictable downstream scaling.
No comparison of fitted exponents, fitting choices, or curve bending.
